concepts.name: How IAM evaluates policies: implicit deny, explicit deny wins

questions.prompt: Your console is set to Asia Pacific (Singapore). You open CloudWatch to create a $5 billing alarm, but there is no **Billing** namespace or `EstimatedCharges` metric. What is the most likely reason?

choices.text: Billing metrics are only published once the account has a paid AWS Support plan
Billing metrics are published per Region, and Singapore has no charges to report on yet
Billing data is only in US East (N. Virginia), and billing alerts must be enabled first
The metric appears only after the account's first monthly invoice has been issued

questions.explanation: CloudWatch stores billing metric data in US East (N. Virginia), and it covers your charges worldwide. You also have to enable billing alerts in Billing preferences before the metric exists; it takes about 15 minutes to appear. The metric is not split per Region, so switching to `us-east-1` is the fix, not waiting for charges in Singapore.

sources.title: Create a billing alarm to monitor your estimated AWS charges
sources.claim: Billing metric data is stored in US East (N. Virginia) and covers worldwide charges; billing alerts must be enabled first and data appears about 15 minutes later.

questions.prompt: On the 3rd of the month your account has spent $2, but usage is on track for $40 by month end. You have a CloudWatch billing alarm on `EstimatedCharges` greater than $5. When does it go into `ALARM`?

choices.text: Only once the estimated charges so far actually exceed $5
Now, because the projected month-end total is above $5
At month end, when the invoice for $40 is generated
Never, because billing alarms only watch free-tier usage

questions.explanation: A CloudWatch billing alarm triggers only when current estimated charges exceed the threshold; it does not use projections. If you want a warning based on the forecast, use AWS Budgets, which can notify on forecasted spend. Neither stops spending by itself, and both lag real usage by hours.

sources.title: Create a billing alarm to monitor your estimated AWS charges
sources.claim: A billing alarm triggers only when current billing exceeds the threshold and doesn't use projections of the month's usage.

sources.title: Managing your costs with AWS Budgets
sources.claim: AWS Budgets can alert on both actual and forecasted spend.

questions.prompt: Why should you set up a billing alarm on the first day you use AWS, and how does a CloudWatch billing alarm differ from an AWS Budgets alert?

model_answer.summary: A billing alarm catches a forgotten or runaway resource before it becomes a large bill. A CloudWatch billing alarm fires on actual estimated charges, while AWS Budgets can also alert on forecasted spend and trigger actions.
key_points: A mistake such as a forgotten instance or a loop calling a paid API keeps costing money until someone notices, so the alarm should exist before you build anything
A CloudWatch billing alarm watches the `EstimatedCharges` metric, which lives in US East (N. Virginia), after you enable billing alerts
The CloudWatch alarm triggers only when current charges pass the threshold, not on projections
AWS Budgets can notify on forecasted as well as actual spend, and can apply actions such as an IAM policy that blocks new resources
Both are delayed by hours and neither is a hard spending cap, so you still have to act on the alert

questions.explanation: The point of a day-one alarm is to limit the damage from mistakes. CloudWatch billing data is updated several times a day and the alarm compares current charges to the threshold. AWS Budgets updates up to three times a day and can look at forecasts. AWS warns that charges can keep growing after a notification, which is why neither tool is a cap.

sources.title: Create a billing alarm to monitor your estimated AWS charges
sources.claim: Estimated charges are sent to CloudWatch several times daily, stored in US East (N. Virginia) after billing alerts are enabled, and the alarm fires only on current charges above the threshold.

sources.title: Managing your costs with AWS Budgets
sources.claim: Budgets alert on actual or forecasted spend, can apply actions such as an IAM policy denying new resources, update up to three times a day, and costs can keep rising after a notification.

questions.prompt: Your `agent-api` container runs on ECS Fargate and needs to read objects from an S3 bucket. What is the recommended way to give it AWS credentials?

choices.text: Create an IAM user, generate access keys, and pass them in environment variables
Copy an access key file into the image at build time
Store the root user's access keys in Secrets Manager and fetch them at startup
Attach an IAM task role; the AWS SDK picks up its temporary credentials automatically

questions.explanation: AWS recommends that workloads use IAM roles with temporary credentials. On AWS compute (EC2, Lambda, ECS) AWS delivers the role's credentials to the resource, and the SDK finds them, so there are no long-lived keys to leak or rotate. IAM user access keys work, but they are long-term credentials and AWS reserves them for cases where roles can't be used.

sources.title: Security best practices in IAM
sources.claim: Workloads should use temporary credentials from IAM roles; on AWS compute AWS delivers the role's credentials and SDKs discover them, so no long-lived IAM user keys are needed.

sources.title: Amazon ECS task IAM role
sources.claim: An ECS task role's permissions are vended to the task's containers, including on Fargate, and the AWS SDK picks up the credentials; it is required to access services such as S3.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between an IAM user and an IAM role. Which would you use for (a) your application running on AWS and (b) a developer signing in to the console, and why?

model_answer.summary: A user is one identity with long-term credentials; a role has no long-term credentials and hands out temporary ones to whoever is allowed to assume it. Use a role for the application, and federation into roles (for example IAM Identity Center) for people.
key_points: An IAM user is tied to one person or workload and can have long-term credentials such as a password or access keys
An IAM role has no long-term credentials; assuming it returns temporary security credentials for a session
A role's trust policy says who may assume it, such as an AWS service, another account, or a federated user
For an application on AWS, attach a role to the compute resource so it gets short-lived credentials automatically

For people, AWS recommends federation with an identity provider so humans also use temporary credentials; IAM users are for cases that can't use roles, such as some third-party tools or emergency access

questions.explanation: The IAM user guide describes a role as assumable by anyone who needs it, with temporary credentials instead of a password or access keys. AWS best practice is temporary credentials for both humans and workloads, which limits the damage when credentials leak because they expire.

sources.title: IAM roles
sources.claim: A role is assumable by anyone who needs it, has no long-term credentials, gives temporary credentials for a session, and its trust policy defines who may assume it; IAM users are for cases federation can't cover, such as emergency access.

sources.title: Security best practices in IAM
sources.claim: Humans should use federation with an identity provider (for example IAM Identity Center) and workloads should use IAM roles, both with temporary credentials.

questions.prompt: A role's identity-based policy allows `s3:*` on `arn:aws:s3:::reports/*`. The `reports` bucket (same account) has a bucket policy that denies `s3:DeleteObject` to all principals. What happens when the role calls `DeleteObject` on `reports/q3.pdf`?

choices.text: Allowed, because the identity-based policy names the bucket explicitly
Denied, because an explicit deny in any applicable policy overrides an allow
Allowed, because identity-based policies are evaluated before resource-based ones
It depends on which of the two policies was attached most recently

questions.explanation: AWS looks for an explicit `Deny` in every applicable policy first: identity-based, resource-based, permissions boundaries, SCPs and session policies. If it finds one, the decision is Deny, whatever the allows say. Order of attachment and how specific the allow is do not matter.

sources.title: How AWS enforcement code logic evaluates requests to allow or deny access
sources.claim: AWS checks SCPs, RCPs, resource-based, identity-based, permissions boundary and session policies for an explicit Deny first, and a single applicable explicit deny gives a final Deny.

sources.title: Policy evaluation logic
sources.claim: Within one account, an explicit deny in either the identity-based or resource-based policy overrides an allow.

questions.prompt: You create a new IAM role with a trust policy but attach no permissions policies. Code running with the role calls `s3:GetObject` on a bucket in the same account that has no bucket policy. What happens?

choices.text: Allowed, because roles can read every bucket in their own account by default
Allowed read-only, because only write actions need an explicit allow
Denied, because every request is implicitly denied unless a policy allows it
The call fails because a role without policies cannot be assumed

questions.explanation: By default all requests are implicitly denied (the root user is the only exception). A request succeeds only if some applicable policy explicitly allows it. The role can still be assumed, since that is governed by its trust policy, but it has no permissions until you attach some.

sources.title: How AWS enforcement code logic evaluates requests to allow or deny access
sources.claim: By default all requests are implicitly denied except for the root user, and a request must be explicitly allowed by a policy.

sources.title: IAM roles
sources.claim: Who can assume a role is set by its trust policy, while its permissions policies define what it can do.

questions.prompt: Your app only needs to read files under `s3://agent-docs/uploads/`. Which permissions policy statement best follows least privilege?

choices.text: `"Action": "s3:GetObject"` on `"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::agent-docs/uploads/*"`
The AWS managed policy `AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess`, which only allows reads
`"Action": "s3:*"` on `"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::agent-docs/*"`
`"Action": "s3:GetObject"` on `"Resource": "*"`

questions.explanation: Least privilege means only the actions needed, on only the resources needed. Option a allows one action on one prefix. The AWS managed read-only policy is tempting, but it allows reading every bucket in the account; AWS notes that managed policies are written for all customers and may not be least privilege for your case. The other two options allow too many actions or too many resources.

sources.title: Security best practices in IAM
sources.claim: Least privilege means granting only the actions needed on specific resources, and AWS managed policies may not be least privilege because they are written for all customers.

questions.prompt: This Lesson's exercise asks you to create an IAM role for your app. Describe how you would set it up so it follows least privilege, and how you would tighten it over time.

model_answer.summary: Create a role that only the app's compute service can assume, grant only the specific actions and resource ARNs the app uses, then use access data to remove anything it doesn't use.
key_points: The trust policy allows only the service that runs the app (for example ECS tasks or Lambda) to assume the role
The permissions policy lists specific actions on specific resource ARNs, not `*`
Conditions can narrow access further, for example requiring TLS
IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from the role's actual activity in CloudTrail, and last-accessed information shows permissions that are never used
Unused permissions are removed as the app matures, and any broad AWS managed policy used at the start is replaced by a customer managed one

questions.explanation: AWS's IAM best practices describe exactly this path: it's fine to start broad while you explore, but move toward least privilege with customer managed policies, conditions, Access Analyzer policy generation, and regular review of unused permissions.

sources.title: Security best practices in IAM
sources.claim: Start broad if needed then move to least privilege with customer managed policies, conditions such as requiring TLS, Access Analyzer policy generation from CloudTrail activity, and last-accessed information to remove unused permissions.

sources.title: Amazon ECS task IAM role
sources.claim: A task role's trust policy names the ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com service, and a role per task definition with minimum permissions is recommended.

questions.prompt: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, who is responsible for applying security patches to the operating system of an EC2 instance that runs your agent?

choices.text: AWS, because it owns the hardware the instance runs on
AWS for critical security patches, you for everything else
Nobody, because EC2 instances are replaced automatically every few hours
You, because the guest operating system is security in the cloud

questions.explanation: AWS is responsible for security of the cloud: facilities, hardware, networking and the software that runs its services. You are responsible for security in the cloud. For EC2 that includes the guest operating system and its patches, the software you install, and security group rules.

sources.title: Shared Responsibility Model - Amazon Web Services (AWS)
sources.claim: AWS protects the infrastructure, while EC2 customers manage the guest operating system including updates and security patches, installed software and the security group firewall.

questions.prompt: You move file storage from a self-managed server on EC2 to Amazon S3. Which responsibility is still yours?

choices.text: Patching the operating system of the servers that run S3
Deciding who can access the data and whether it's encrypted
Replacing failed disks in the S3 data centres
None: with a managed service AWS takes on all security

questions.explanation: With managed services like S3, AWS runs the infrastructure and platform, so your share shrinks, but it never reaches zero. You still manage your data: its classification, encryption choices, and the IAM and bucket policies that decide who can read it. Most S3 data leaks come from permissions the customer set.

sources.title: Shared Responsibility Model - Amazon Web Services (AWS)
sources.claim: For abstracted services like S3, AWS runs the infrastructure, OS and platform, and customers manage their data including encryption options, classify assets and use IAM tools for permissions.
